title: How can we identify distinct crew-hiring patterns to improve recruitment recommendations for student filmmakers?
s2_title: Student filmmakers search for crew in three distinct ways, and how they search predicts how hard the role is to fill
segs: How they search: only their own circle; 82% asked someone they already knew, 55% someone they had worked with, and no other channel
Results: easiest to fill (7.3 out of 10, where 10 = very easy); hires rated 9.5 out of 10; 91% would hire again; 1 of 11 roles had a last-minute dropout
How they search: in public; 80% posted Instagram ISOs, 80% asked for referrals, only 1 of 10 asked someone they knew. Mostly specialist and support roles (art, gaffer, grip, colorist, makeup)
Results: moderately hard to fill (5.1 out of 10); hires rated 7.4; 80% would hire again; no dropouts
How they search: every channel at once; all asked classmates and people they knew, 7 of 8 also asked for referrals. 5 of 8 were senior or advanced productions
Results: hardest to fill (4.1 out of 10); hires rated 7.5; 63% would hire again; 3 of 8 roles had a last-minute dropout
proof_title: Proof: the three patterns are real
proof: a clustering model (k-means) sorted the 29 hires into groups of similar hires using only how the producer searched: the 5 most used search methods. Ease of finding, ratings and dropouts were left out, so they are a fair check on the groups.
the chart shows how much hires still differ from their group (lower = tighter). Three groups cut that from 100 to 34, a 66% drop; each extra group after that helps by 8 or less.
Does it hold for new hires?
We hid 9 of the 29 hires (about 30%) while building the groups, then sorted them in afterwards. Three groups described them 37% better than one group for everyone (50.4 → 31.6).
the model never saw ease of finding, yet the groups split cleanly on it (7.3 vs 5.1 vs 4.1 out of 10). A gap this large would happen by chance less than 4% of the time.
our NYU Student Film Crewing Survey, answered Oct–Nov 2026 about past productions: 10 producers, 29 hires.
s3_title: Matching each poster’s discover page to their hiring pattern puts help where the search time is: Open search and Scramble hold 76% of it
how: The app looks at how they searched for their past hires and places them in their closest hiring pattern
Their discover page is built for that pattern
example: Producer 6 posts a job. Past hires (DP, UPM, art director) were found through classmates, people they knew and referrals → Scramble → curated shortlist first. Those roles were in fact hard to fill: 1 to 3 out of 10.
pages: They already have people; a shortlist saves only 1.4 hours a post
Discovery feed of new candidates matched to the role
They need strangers; a shortlist saves 2.5 hours a post
Curated shortlist first, then the discovery feed
Hardest to fill; a shortlist saves 2.9 hours a post
ease: Each producer rated how easy it was to find a qualified person for each role (1–10), for hires made before our app. On a marketplace it still differs: some roles are scarce (drivers, art assistants) and some producers have a network to fall back on. Once the app has users, v2 replaces the survey rating with the app’s own data: applicants per post, days to fill, and how often posters re-book past crew.
value_title: What it is worth (29 surveyed hires)
value_text: Shortlists go to a pattern only while they pay for themselves: Trusted network up to $27 a post, Open search up to $49, Scramble up to $59. At $25 that is everyone; if shortlists cost $40, Trusted network drops out and matching wins.
foot: How the numbers work (fictional assumptions): a role takes 1 hour of searching per point of difficulty (10 − ease); a curated shortlist halves that; a producer hour is worth $20; a shortlist costs the app $25. Net value = hours saved × $20 − shortlist cost. Each hire’s page is set only from that producer’s other hires, so the model never sees the hire it is judged on.
